items.note: It answers the question directly: the timing and size suggest the price increase drove Pro churn, but this isn't proven. My recount matches its figures: Pro churn went from 1/16 before July to 8/15 after, against 1/16 to 3/15 for Basic.
It never says it excluded trials, but the counts show it did. Including the 12 Mar–Jun Pro trial accounts would change the 16-account Pro denominator, and 16 is the correct non-trial count.

The @ourco.test QA accounts (1056–1060, all July Pro signups that cancelled in Aug) are left out. The July Pro cohort is reported as 2 of 4, which is correct only without them, and the August count of 7 also excludes them.
A blank cancel_month is read as still active, and any cancel_month counts as churn. All the tallies follow this rule.

This isn't written for a CEO. It opens with a long data-quality note about the price column instead of the answer. It also uses analyst terms a CEO wouldn't need, such as Fisher exact test, one-sided and two-sided p-values, at-risk denominators, and column names.

The summary has 5 top-level bullets, but the third one holds 5 more nested sub-bullets, so about 10 in total. Each bullet is also a dense paragraph. That goes beyond the intent of 'at most 5 bullets'.
It suggests one specific chart: grouped bars of Pro vs Basic churn rate, before and after July, with count labels and a line marking the price change.
It rates confidence as moderate-to-low and gives the reasons: a small sample (31 accounts, 11 Pro churners), p ≈ 0.13, and other possible explanations.
